As of August 1, 2026, bitcoin:native is trading at $62,956, down 49.41% from the cycle peak set on October 6, 2025. The median trajectory of the three previous cycles at the same number of days after the peak points to $45,347. This means the current price is 39% above the historical median scenario, so Bitcoin is holding up noticeably better than in previous cycles.

The $45K level is not a target and does not mean the market will necessarily return to it, but it shows that the current cycle is unfolding much more mildly than the historical scenario and retains relative strength, although this gap alone does not confirm that the decline is over or that a bottom has formed.

Strategy Inc (MSTR) Q2 FY2026 earnings call transcript

TL;DR

Strategy is no longer a company that directs all available funds into Bitcoin under any circumstances. After the problems with STRC, management acknowledged that keeping the U.S. dollar reserve too low was a mistake.

The new model is built around active management of three elements: Bitcoin, U.S. dollars, and digital credit. The company will continue buying BTC, but it will also sell it to fund dividends, reserves, and securities buybacks. The main short-term objective is to bring STRC back to $100 and restore confidence among credit investors.

The fundamental thesis has not changed: Strategy wants to use Bitcoin as capital, issue digital credit against it, and increase Bitcoin per share through that model. But the execution of the strategy has become more cautious, countercyclical, and dependent on market conditions.

10/10

The main conclusion:

The market is entering a regime of inflationary economic slowdown combined with tighter monetary policy.

This is an unfavorable environment for expensive, highly leveraged assets that depend on future growth. The main risk is that the energy shock, interest rates, trade restrictions, and geopolitics are beginning to reinforce one another.

9/10

Strong manufacturing data may be misleading.

A significant share of the growth is being driven not by sustainable demand, but by inventory accumulation ahead of possible supply disruptions. Once this cycle ends, manufacturing activity could slow sharply.

8/10

China remains dependent on exports.

Domestic demand, real estate, retail sales, and investment are weak, while technology exports are growing rapidly. This model is becoming increasingly vulnerable to new tariffs and restrictions from the US and EU.

7/10

The ECB has already raised rates. The Bank of Japan increased its rate to 1% - the highest level since 1995.

The largest developed economies are tightening policy at the same time. This reduces global liquidity and puts pressure on asset valuations.

6/10

The energy shock has already spread beyond the oil market.

Rising prices for oil, gas, fertilizers, transportation, and semiconductor components are feeding into core inflation. Even lower oil prices would not guarantee a rapid return of inflation to normal levels.

5/10

Rates are not the only problem.

Companies are starting to limit AI usage because of the high cost of these services. Chip prices are rising, while the returns on massive investments are becoming less certain.

The AI bubble has not burst yet, but its foundations have weakened.

4/10

The main victims of the new regime are highly valued technology and AI companies.

Higher rates reduce the present value of future earnings and increase the cost of servicing the debt used to finance AI infrastructure.

3/10

New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has abandoned traditional forward guidance.

Markets will now have to focus on the data rather than a pre-signaled path for interest rates. This increases uncertainty and could raise the risk premium.

2/10

The Fed kept rates unchanged but effectively shifted toward a more hawkish stance.

The probability of at least one rate hike by the end of 2026 has risen to 88.2%. The reason is inflation: PCE reached 4.1%, while core PCE rose to 3.8%.

1/10

The global economy is entering a dangerous regime: inflation remains high, central banks are tightening policy, and geopolitical risks are intensifying.
